items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: when I first joined the Count Basie band in 1938, Lester Young, he was my roommate.

ctx.x: And we are interested in hearing your stories and, of course where you got your nickname, we have to ask that, but—

Well when I first joined the Count Basie band in 1938, Lester Young, he was my roommate. And he had a knack for giving names to people that always stuck. So he gave me the name of “Sweets.” He gave Billie Holiday the name of “Lady Day,” and he named himself “Prez.”

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: playing with Basie’s band, playing with Lester and Jo Jones and those guys

ctx.x: No. When I first joined the band, they didn’t have no music. We used to take turns in carrying the whole repertoire which was in one little portfolio. Everybody would carry it but Prez. Prez wouldn’t carry it. Then I sort of got depressed playing with Basie’s band, playing with Lester and Jo Jones and those guys, that was the epitome to me of musicians. They were amazing every night. Prez played something different every night, Buck would play something different. It was just amazing. God blessed me when I went…
How long were you with the band before you started to feel this need for something…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: He named me 'Sweets.' ... He named himself 'Pres.' ... he had a knack for doing so many things that were comical in the band.

ctx.x: That's what's absurd today, isn't it, about inflation?

That's for sure. 50 cents, I remember one time Pres used to be the first one off the bus to get a room. And while we were all trying to get ourselves together, he would probably be up in the room asleep, you know. And he went to get his room and all of a sudden he came down the steps rushing and cursing. I said, "What's wrong, Pres?" He said, "The room rent went up from 35 cents to 50 cents and I checked out," you know. He checked out. That was funny, because she went up 15 cents on the room.

There was no hotel, we would stay in the private homes, you know. A woman would have a big house, a boarding house, five or six rooms. So five or six guys would stay here and then four or five would stay someplace else, you know. So -- but Columbus was sort of a mecca for the big bands in those days. They had so many. They had places downtown the whites, you know, theater.
